Editorial reviews artificial intelligence reliability gaps across smart grids and cities

An editorial published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence examining twelve research contributions reports a persistent operational gap between high artificial intelligence benchmark scores in controlled laboratories and reliable performance in real-world smart environments. While artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed across intelligent cities and next-generation power grids to bolster security, resilience, and operational autonomy, laboratory evaluations often fail to ensure real-world utility. The authors observe that an attack-detection model may successfully flag an intrusion yet leave operators without clear guidance on how to respond, while predictive-maintenance systems trained to anticipate equipment breakdowns at one utility frequently fail to generalize when transferred to another facility.

The Research Topic collection addresses the technical and governance threshold required before automated model outputs can be trusted to alter operational services. Contextualizing these challenges within recent literature, the editorial notes that Kumar and De reviewed deep reinforcement learning architectures designed for power-system resilience, whereas Wolniak and Stecuła evaluated artificial intelligence implementations and institutional adoption barriers across municipal governance and urban services. Furthermore, Li and colleagues linked algorithmic robustness, privacy protection, fairness, and institutional accountability across the complete lifecycle of artificial intelligence.

Together, the surveyed publications demonstrate that technical detection results frequently depend on specific test environments, model retraining can unintentionally sacrifice system stability for responsiveness, and effective interventions can conflict with overarching operational priorities. To structure these challenges, the editorial introduces a conceptual framework that maps transitions between detection, adaptation, intervention, and recovery. The authors emphasize that this framework connects three decisions typically analyzed in isolation: determining whether a detected anomaly warrants physical action, deciding whether operational models require retraining, and evaluating whether an automated intervention genuinely improves service health rather than introducing collateral disruptions.

Investigating detection capabilities, several contributions demonstrated that machine learning efficacy fluctuates significantly across benchmark datasets. Ilias and colleagues documented peak intrusion-detection accuracy reaching 99.96 percent on the 5G-NIDD benchmark dataset, but that performance dropped to 79.59 percent when evaluated against the NANCY dataset, underscoring the strong sensitivity of benchmark outcomes to experimental conditions. In complementary networking evaluations, Balakrishnan and Maddikunta achieved 97.32 percent detection accuracy on the CICIoT2023 dataset with a rapid inference latency of 0.219 milliseconds per sample, though the transferability of this model to diverse real-world network traffic environments remains unverified.

In municipal public safety domains, Altayeva and Omarov demonstrated competitive acoustic detection performance across two public sound benchmarks while maintaining a smaller computational footprint than baseline comparison architectures. Concurrently, Zhukabayeva and co-authors recorded a macro F1 score of 0.962 on a closed-circuit television dataset, using visual explanation techniques to inspect model predictions for municipal surveillance. However, drawing on findings from an intrusion-detection preprint by Subasi and colleagues, the editorial cautions that feature explanations often vary substantially across different analytical methods and training configurations, meaning an alert and its explanation must be operationally validated to confirm whether they reliably help operators distinguish genuine emergencies from false alarms.

Addressing the challenge of training models across physically separated sites and shifting operational conditions, Ghosh and Mittal evaluated decentralized federated learning frameworks using heterogeneous datasets collected from electrical substation equipment. Their comparative analysis established that federated batch normalization yielded the highest performance, achieving an F-score of 0.88 across substation monitoring tasks. In a parallel investigation of cybersecurity across distributed edge nodes, El-Hajj and Zeineddine paired federated malware detection with drift-triggered retraining mechanisms, observing that classification accuracy declined markedly when entire attack experiments were withheld during testing compared to conventional random evaluation splits.

In energy analytics, Zhao and colleagues developed methods that minimized spurious fluctuations in electricity-use profiles while improving the detection of genuine behavioral shifts relative to baseline algorithms, while a systematic review by Marín Vásquez and colleagues identified nine software and Internet of Things technologies capable of supporting knowledge transfer in industrial maintenance. The editorial authors stress that variations across physical sites and operational changes over time necessitate distinct diagnostic procedures. Because federated systems face privacy and adversarial risks as noted by Mengistu and Zhang, site-level validation and update safeguards are required, and drift alerts must prompt root-cause investigation before retraining, distinguishing between structural demand evolution and physical sensor malfunctions.

Examining commercial applications and municipal planning, Anand and Grama utilized empirical data across ten United States states to optimize electric vehicle charging network layouts. Their computational optimization models estimated a 52.3 percent reduction in average travel distance to charging stations alongside a 71.7 percent reduction in overloaded facilities relative to existing spatial distributions. While these numerical estimates provide valuable preliminary screening metrics for infrastructure investment, municipal planners and grid operators must weigh real-world capital expenses, land acquisition costs, and local grid connection constraints against projected station utilization before allocating funds.

In related organizational research, Hawash and colleagues showed that integrating user behavior and group attributes into semantic matching improved recommendation rankings, though long-term participation effects remain unmeasured. Examining governance structures, Aljuaidi and colleagues identified threat intelligence integration, crisis leadership, and automated artificial intelligence monitoring as the top three drivers of organizational cyber resilience. To operationalize safety protocols, Kindong and colleagues formulated the Prevent-Audit-Learn-Harden lifecycle framework to assign specific responsibilities to system actors in energy management, aligning with auditability frameworks proposed by Li and Goel.

To bridge the gap between algorithmic prediction and physical operations, the editorial outlines three strategic research priorities. First, researchers must rigorously assess model transferability across novel sites, later operating periods, and unseen attack scenarios while comparing retraining costs against data-quality remediation. Second, supervised operational pilots must measure the tangible consequences of acting on algorithmic predictions, tracking physical metrics such as utility downtime, unnecessary maintenance work orders, dispatch delays, and false alarm dispatches. Finally, controlled failure exercises must evaluate recovery dynamics during sensor loss, corrupted updates, and emergency rollback procedures, ensuring that automated systems enhance whole-system resilience rather than inducing unintended infrastructure interruptions.
